title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbook, benchmarking suite, release notes, known issues, and runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling guidance, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite description, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the canonical reference for the eng-serving-runtime team and SREs responsible for production inference fleets. The goal is to make performance tuning and incident response repeatable and low-risk.

Table of contents
1) Runtime architecture overview
2) Kernel scheduling and policy definitions
3) Profiling playbook (how-to)
4) Benchmarking suite and CI integration
5) Recent release notes (summary)
6) Known issues and workarounds
7) Runtime runbooks (incident procedures)
8) Team wiki and ownership

1) Runtime architecture overview

Short summary: The serving runtime is composed of a small set of services designed for predictable latency, efficient GPU utilization, and graceful degradation. Key components: 
- API Gateway (service: redwood-api-gw) — REST/HTTP+gRPC front door, enforces rate limits, auth, and routing to model routes. Owner: eng-platform.
- Router / Smart Router (service: runtime-router) — request policy evaluation (latency vs cost), region/zone affinity, and model variant selection. Owner: serving runtime core.
- Scheduler / Batch Manager (service: batch-scheduler) — aggregates individual requests into execution batches. Responsible for batch size caps, max wait windows and continuous batching. Owner: serving runtime core.
- Model Worker / Runner (service: model-runner) — per-GPU worker process that executes compiled kernels and manages KV cache. Supports multi-tenant on-dedicated pools and private deployments. Owner: serving runtime core.
- KV Cache Service (embedded component in model-runner) — prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts.
- Telemetry & Tracing (services: obs-forwarder, trace-collector) — collects token-level metrics, GPU counters, and traces. Owner: observability.
- Control plane (service: runtime-control-plane) — deployments, rollouts, model catalog, quantization profiles. Owner: eng-platform/product.

SLOs and operational targets (summary table):
| SLO / Metric | Target | Owner | Notes |
|--------------|--------|-------|-------|
| p50 latency (text gen, 512 ctx) | < 60 ms | eng-serving-runtime | median under typical traffic |
| p95 latency (text gen, 2k ctx) | < 220 ms | eng-serving-runtime | includes queueing |
| Tail latency (99.9) | < 2s | eng-sre | triggered fallback to cheaper variant |
| Throughput (tokens/sec per GPU) | see benchmark profiles | eng-serving-runtime | varies by model & quantization |

Networking & ports: model-runners accept internal gRPC on 127.0.0.1:19000 for control and 0.0.0.0:19100 for worker pool. Router and scheduler communicate over TLS. See infra-standards for CIDR allocations.

2) Kernel scheduling and policy definitions

Objectives: maximize amortized GPU throughput while meeting per-request latency SLOs and preserving QoS for high-priority tenants. Key knobs: batching window (max_wait_ms), max_batch_size, concurrency limit (max_concurrent_sequences), kernel preference (fp16/int8), stream affinity.

Recommended defaults (by GPU class and workload):
- A100 (long-context generative workloads)
  - max_wait_ms: 20
  - max_batch_size: 48
  - max_concurrent_sequences: 6 (per worker)
  - preferred_quant: fp16 or q4f16 for 8k contexts
- H100 (high throughput, short-context classification/embeddings)
  - max_wait_ms: 8
  - max_batch_size: 96
  - max_concurrent_sequences: 12
  - preferred_quant: fp16/q4_0

Policy definitions (examples):
- Latency-first policy: enforce max_wait_ms=5ms, smaller batches, route to low-load workers. Use for interactive chat endpoints with p95 <= 150ms requirement.
- Cost-first policy: increase max_wait_ms up to 50ms and larger batches; fallback to cheaper quantized model if queue depth > 200.
- Mixed policy: dynamic policy that increases batch size during sustained high QPS but lowers it when p95 approaches SLO.

Kernel selection: the runtime chooses kernels by matching (model_arch, seq_len, quant_profile, gpu_arch). The kernel selector table (maintained in control plane config) has entries keyed by model signature and a scored list of kernel/provider combos. Example selector fragment (YAML-like example):

# kernel-selector.yaml (example)
# order: higher score preferred
models:
  - name: rwkv-8k
    signatures: [transformer, causal]
    kernels:
      - provider: native-cuda
        quant: fp16
        max_seq: 8192
        score: 100
      - provider: fused-attn-kernel-v2
        quant: q4f16
        max_seq: 4096
        score: 90

Tuning tips: when p95 spikes but GPUs show <70% utilization, reduce max_wait_ms by 25% and limit max_batch_size to current 75th percentile batch size. If GPUs are saturated and tail latency is unacceptable, prefer using a slightly lower-accuracy kernel with faster memory access (e.g., fused attention v2).

3) Profiling playbook (how-to)

Purpose: provide reproducible steps to profile a model route and identify kernel hotspots, memory fragmentation, and host-GPU synchronization issues.

Prerequisites: access to the run that reproduces the issue, GPU node with profiling tools installed (nsys, nvprof/nvtx, nsys, nvidia-smi), and a test workload that approximates production traffic.

Steps:
1) Reproduce a small representative trace (10-100 requests) against the exact model version. Use request-replay tool: bin/replay-requests --route <route> --count 50 --seed 42 --concurrency 4.
2) Capture system-level metrics: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.total,memory.used --format=csv -l 1 (during the run).
3) If kernel-level detail is required, run NVIDIA Nsight Systems: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=profile-report ./bin/runner --config test-config.yaml
4) For PyTorch-based kernels, capture profiler trace: python -m torch.profiler --schedule "wait=1,warmup=1,active=3" --output-profile profile.pt -- python serve_trace.py
5) Correlate traces with token-level timings from obs-forwarder (token timing fields: token_enqueue_time, kernel_start_time, kernel_end_time). Pull traces with: curl -s "https://obs.internal/api/traces?trace_id=<id>" | jq .
6) Identify hotspots: long host-to-device memcpy, synchronization points, underfilled kernels (batch sizes << configured max_batch_size).
7) Iterate on kernel parameters in a staging lane and re-run the profile. Document improvements as regression tests.

Common profiling commands and diagnostic heuristics:
- High host CPU usage + low GPU utilization => investigate batching delay or slow serialization.
- High memcpy times => check NUMA, CPU pinning, PCIe topology, and use CUDA IPC where possible.
- Many small kernels with low occupancy => consider fused kernels or larger batch targets.

4) Benchmarking suite and CI integration

Benchmark suite objectives: produce stable, reproducible numbers for latency p50/p95/p99, throughput (tokens/sec), GPU memory usage, and cost-per-1000-tokens estimate across model variants and quantization profiles. Benchmarks are stored in the repo: infra/benchmarks/serving-runtime and executed in CI via the bench-runner job.

Suite components:
- microbench (kernel-level latency & op throughput)
- routebench (end-to-end route performance with realistic traffic shapes)
- coldstartbench (container cold start + model load)
- membench (peak memory / fragmentation tests)

How to run locally (example):
- Checkout infra/benchmarks and create a test VM with the same GPU class.
- Run: ./bench-runner --suite routebench --config bench-configs/gpt-like-2k.yaml --output results/2026-08-01.json

CI practices:
- All runtime changes that touch scheduling or kernels must include a bench-runner tag. The CI job runs routebench and membench on a representative A100 instance.
- Benchmarks are compared against a baseline.json stored in infra/benchmarks/baselines. Any regression > 5% on p95 or throughput must be triaged and explained in the PR.

Expected baseline examples (informational):
- gpt-small (2k ctx) on A100, fp16: p50=38ms, p95=140ms, throughput=1500 tok/s
- gpt-medium (8k ctx) on A100, q4f16: p50=120ms, p95=420ms, throughput=650 tok/s

5) Recent release notes (summary)

Release: serving-runtime v1.8.2 (released 2026-07-30)
Highlights:
- Improved kernel selector scoring to prefer fused-attn-v2 for short contexts, reducing p95 by ~12% on average.
- New dynamic batching window: adaptive_wait_ms feature toggled by route policy.
- Fixed a memory leak in KV cache for incremental prefix caching (bug id: SR-2026-113).
- Bench-runner updates: added membench tests for quantized models.

Upgrade notes:
- Rolling upgrade recommended: canary 10% -> 50% -> 100% with 15m observation window per step. Watch p95 and error rate.

6) Known issues and workarounds

- SR-2026-135 — Occasional p99 spikes for 8k-context models on A100 when concurrent sequence count > 10. Workaround: temporarily lower max_concurrent_sequences to 6 and enable adaptive_wait_ms. Root cause: kernel contention in shared L2 paths.
- SR-2026-142 — Model-runner process may report increasing resident set size over weeks on specific quantization profiles. Workaround: periodic process recycle via rolling restart (staggered 5m) and upgrade to v1.8.2 where a leak is patched (see SR-2026-113).
- SR-2026-150 — Some embeddings routes experience elevated latency after autoscaler scales nodes down. Workaround: configure cooldown window to 10m and maintain minimum pool size for high-priority routes.

7) Runtime runbooks (incident procedures)

Runbook: High p95 latency on a production route
1) Triage: confirm alerts (pager duty) and gather metrics: curl https://obs.internal/api/metrics?route=<route>&window=15m
2) Check router queue depths and scheduler backlog: kubectl -n runtime get pods -l app=batch-scheduler -o wide && kubectl logs -l app=batch-scheduler --tail 200
3) Validate GPU health: ssh node && nvidia-smi --query-gpu=timestamp,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu,memory.used --format=csv -l 1 &
4) If GPUs underutilized (<60%) and queue depth high: reduce max_wait_ms for the route to 10ms and notify via workflow: bin/runtime-config set-policy --route <route> --max_wait_ms 10 --reason "p95 spike mitigation"
5) If GPUs saturated (>90%) and tail latency high: temporarily route traffic to fallback model variant (lower memory / quantized) using control-plane rollout: bin/control-plane promote-variant --route <route> --variant <fallback> --percentage 30
6) If system OOM or runaway memory: initiate rolling restart of affected model-runners: kubectl rollout restart deployment/model-runner --field-selector metadata.name=<node subset> --timeout=10m. Monitor memory after restart.
7) Escalate to oncall runtime core if changes required beyond config knobs.

Runbook: Model-runner OOM on startup
1) Confirm pod crashed: kubectl -n runtime get pods --selector app=model-runner -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, status: .status.phase}'
2) Inspect crash loop logs: kubectl logs <pod> -p
3) Check model binary/quant profile compatibility: bin/validate-model --model-id <id> --profile <quant_profile>
4) If incompatible profile detected, revert to previous quant_profile in control plane and redeploy.
5) If memory demand legitimately exceeds node capacity, scale up node type or use a different allocation pool.
6) Contact runtime core lead if root cause is unknown: paged person: Miguel Santos (pager duty: eng-serving-runtime-primary).
